subChunks.title: Threads & Runnable
subChunks.hookHtml: Two apprentices trying to cast spells simultaneously — but they keep interrupting each other, corrupting the arcane weave. Welcome to the world of concurrency, where mastering threads means mastering chaos itself.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Creating Threads

Java represents a thread of execution with the Thread class. You can create one by subclassing it or — more commonly — by passing a Runnable to its constructor.

// Subclassing Thread (less preferred)
class SpellThread extends Thread {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Spell cast from thread: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}

// Starting it
SpellThread t = new SpellThread();
t.start(); // Do NOT call run() directly — that executes on the current thread!

Runnable vs Thread Subclass

Prefer Runnable because Java has single inheritance — subclassing Thread prevents you from extending another class. Runnable is a functional interface, so lambdas work perfectly.

Runnable spellTask = () -> {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        System.out.println("Casting from: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
};

Thread t = new Thread(spellTask, "SpellThread-1");
t.start();
t.join(); // Wait for t to finish before continuing

Thread Lifecycle

A thread moves through these states: NEW (created but not started), RUNNABLE (executing or ready to execute), BLOCKED (waiting for a monitor lock), WAITING (waiting indefinitely for another thread), TIMED_WAITING (waiting for a specified time — e.g. Thread.sleep(100)), and TERMINATED (finished).

Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(50); // TIMED_WAITING state
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
});
System.out.println(t.getState()); // NEW
t.start();
System.out.println(t.getState()); // RUNNABLE or TIMED_WAITING
t.join();
System.out.println(t.getState()); // TERMINATED

Race Conditions

When two threads read and write a shared variable without coordination, results become unpredictable. This is a race condition.

class Counter {
    int count = 0; // shared, unprotected!
    void increment() { count++; } // NOT atomic: read, add, write = 3 steps
}

Counter c = new Counter();
Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i=0;i<500;i++) c.increment(); });
Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i=0;i<500;i++) c.increment(); });
t1.start(); t2.start();
t1.join();  t2.join();
System.out.println(c.count); // Could be anything from 500 to 1000!

The synchronized Keyword

synchronized ensures only one thread executes a block at a time by acquiring a monitor lock. You can apply it to methods or explicit blocks.

class SafeCounter {
    private int count = 0;

    // Synchronized method — lock is the SafeCounter instance
    synchronized void increment() {
        count++;
    }

    // Synchronized block — more granular, better for performance
    void incrementBlock() {
        synchronized (this) {
            count++;
        }
    }

    int getCount() { return count; }
}

// volatile: guarantees visibility across threads (reads/writes go to main memory)
// Use when one thread writes, others only read — NOT for compound operations
private volatile boolean running = true;

storyBeats.text: Deep in the Academy's twin spell-chambers, two apprentices attempt to cast simultaneously. The arcane weave flickers and stutters — their incantations are colliding.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Every great mage eventually faces the challenge of wielding two spells at once. In the arcane arts — and in Java — we call this concurrency.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A Thread is an independent path of execution. Like two apprentices casting in separate chambers — they run concurrently, but must not interfere with each other's materials.

storyBeats.speaker: Thread Creation
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But beware — when two threads reach for the same magical artifact simultaneously, chaos erupts. We call this a race condition.

storyBeats.speaker: The Fix: synchronized
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But synchronized is a heavy tool. For simpler coordination — when one thread writes a flag and others only read it — use volatile. It guarantees that every thread sees the latest written value, bypassing any CPU cache. The catch: volatile does not make compound operations atomic. count++ is three steps — read, add, write — so volatile alone cannot protect a counter. Use synchronized or AtomicInteger for that.

storyBeats.speaker: volatile flag

storyBeats.text: With synchronization woven into the spell, the two apprentices take turns touching the arcane counter — no collision, no corruption, a perfect 1000.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
First, create two threads: Thread A prints "Spell A casting..." 3 times and Thread B prints "Spell B casting..." 3 times. Start both threads, then call join() on each to wait for completion.

Then demonstrate safe synchronization: create a static inner class SpellCounter with a synchronized void increment() method and an int count field. Launch two threads that each call increment() 500 times, join both, and print counter.count. The result must be exactly 1000.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a race condition is and why simply making a method 'synchronized' prevents it. What exactly does 'acquiring the monitor lock' mean, and what happens to other threads that try to enter a synchronized block while the lock is held?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, write a program with a static inner class SpellCounter that has a synchronized void increment() method. Create two threads that each increment the counter 500 times. Join both threads and print the final count. Also create a thread using a lambda Runnable that prints "Spell A casting..." three times and another that prints "Spell B casting..." three times, starting and joining both.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Every Java object has an intrinsic lock (monitor). The synchronized keyword acquires this lock, guaranteeing mutual exclusion for threads.
A keyword that ensures a variable's value is always read from and written to main memory, preventing threads from caching stale values — but does NOT ensure atomicity for compound operations.
Blocks the calling thread until the target thread terminates. Essential for coordinating results from background threads.
A situation where two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs, and neither can proceed. Avoided by always acquiring locks in the same order.
Java threads move through NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, and TERMINATED states, queryable via Thread.getState().
Thrown when a thread is waiting or sleeping and another thread calls interrupt() on it. Always restore the interrupt flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() in catch blocks.
A JVM memory model guarantee: actions in one thread that 'happen-before' another are visible to that thread. synchronized and volatile both establish happens-before relationships.
Similar to deadlock but threads keep changing state in response to each other without making progress — like two people in a hallway each stepping aside in the same direction indefinitely.

questions.questionHtml: Which method actually starts a new OS-level thread in Java?
options: Thread.run()
Thread.start()
Thread.execute()
Thread.launch()
questions.explanationHtml: start() creates a new thread and invokes run() on it. Calling run() directly executes it on the current thread — no new thread is created.

questions.questionHtml: What is the guaranteed output of this code (ignoring thread scheduling order)?
questions.explanationHtml: The synchronized keyword ensures inc() is atomic. Both threads each call it 3 times, guaranteeing a final count of 6.

questions.questionHtml: This code is supposed to print the counter result after both threads finish, but it sometimes prints 0 or an intermediate value. What is wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: join() is never called, so the main thread prints count before t1 and t2 finish
questions.explanationHtml: The main thread prints count immediately after calling start(), without waiting for threads to finish. Fix: call t1.join(); t2.join(); before the print. Additionally, count++ is not atomic, so synchronized or AtomicInteger is also needed.

options: When multiple threads perform compound operations like check-then-act on the variable
When one thread writes a boolean flag and other threads only read it
When you need to ensure only one thread executes a critical section at a time
When incrementing a counter from multiple threads
questions.correctAnswer: When one thread writes a boolean flag and other threads only read it
questions.explanationHtml: volatile guarantees visibility (no stale caches) but NOT atomicity. It's perfect for a simple flag one thread flips and others read. For compound operations like count++, use synchronized or AtomicInteger.

subChunks.title: ExecutorService & Thread Pools
subChunks.hookHtml: Creating a new thread for every task is like hiring a new apprentice for every single spell — exhausting and wasteful. Thread pools let you reuse a fixed team of workers efficiently.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why Thread Pools?

Creating and destroying threads is expensive. A thread pool maintains a set of pre-created threads. Tasks are submitted to a queue; idle threads pick them up. This caps resource usage and eliminates thread-creation overhead.

// Bad: new thread per task
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    new Thread(task).start(); // 100 threads created and destroyed!
}

// Good: reuse a pool of 4 threads
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    pool.submit(task); // queued and picked up by idle threads
}
pool.shutdown();

Callable vs Runnable

Runnable.run() returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions. Callable<V>.call() returns a value and can throw any exception — making it the right choice when you need a result.

Callable<String> spellTask = () -> {
    // do work...
    return "Fireball complete";
};

Future<String> future = pool.submit(spellTask);
String result = future.get(); // blocks until result available
System.out.println(result); // "Fireball complete"

Future & Blocking

Future.get() blocks the calling thread until the task completes. You can also provide a timeout: future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) to avoid waiting forever. future.isDone() checks without blocking.

Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> 42);
System.out.println(f.isDone()); // might be false
int val = f.get();              // blocks, then returns 42
System.out.println(f.isDone()); // true

Shutdown Lifecycle

Always shut down your executor. shutdown() stops accepting new tasks but lets queued tasks finish. shutdownNow() attempts to cancel running tasks. awaitTermination() blocks until all tasks complete or timeout occurs.

pool.shutdown();
try {
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
        pool.shutdownNow(); // force if still running after 10s
    }
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    pool.shutdownNow();
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
}

Other Executor Flavors

Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() — one thread, tasks run sequentially in submission order. Executors.newCachedThreadPool() — creates new threads as needed, reuses idle ones (unbounded — use with caution). Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n) — for delayed or periodic tasks.

// Single-threaded: guaranteed sequential execution
ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
single.submit(() -> System.out.println("Task 1"));
single.submit(() -> System.out.println("Task 2")); // always after Task 1
single.shutdown();

storyBeats.text: The Academy's arcane factory hums with activity. Rather than summoning new apprentices for every minor enchantment, the Archmage has established a permanent team of skilled spell-workers.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Raw thread creation is like hiring a fresh apprentice, training them, and then dismissing them after one spell. Ruinously inefficient. A thread pool keeps trained workers ready at all times.

storyBeats.speaker: Creating a Pool
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A Callable is like a Runnable that returns a receipt — a Future — proving the spell was cast and recording the outcome. Call get() on that Future when you need the result.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And always, always shut down the pool when work is done. An executor left running is like leaving cauldrons boiling unattended — a disaster waiting to happen.

storyBeats.speaker: Proper Shutdown
storyBeats.text:
pool.shutdown();
pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

With the thread pool established, the Academy dispatches five enchantment tasks. Three workers grab the first three immediately; the remaining two wait their turn in the queue — orderly, efficient, and safe.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Create a newFixedThreadPool(3). Submit 5 Callable<String> tasks — each returns "Spell-N completed" where N is 1 through 5. Collect all 5 Future<String> objects into a list, then call get() on each and print the result. Finally call shutdown() and awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between Callable and Runnable, and why Future.get() can be dangerous if called without a timeout. What is the difference between shutdown() and shutdownNow(), and when would you use each?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, create a fixed thread pool of 3 threads, submit 5 Callable tasks returning "Spell-N completed" (N = 1-5), collect all Futures, print each result via get(), then properly shut down the pool with shutdown() and awaitTermination().

rabbitHoleTerms.description: An interface extending Executor that manages a pool of threads. Provides submit(), invokeAll(), invokeAny(), shutdown(), and awaitTermination() among others.
Represents the result of an asynchronous computation. get() blocks until the result is available; cancel() attempts to cancel the task.
Like Runnable but its call() method returns a value of type V and can throw checked exceptions. Used with ExecutorService.submit().
CPU-bound tasks: pool size = number of CPU cores. I/O-bound tasks: pool size can be larger since threads spend time waiting. Rule of thumb: measure under realistic load.
Thrown when a task is submitted to a pool after shutdown() has been called or the queue is full.
Executors.newWorkStealingPool() uses a ForkJoinPool where idle threads steal tasks from busy threads' queues — useful for uneven workloads.
Submits a collection of Callables and blocks until all complete, returning a list of Futures. Unlike submitting individually, it waits for ALL tasks.
After calling shutdown(), this blocks the calling thread until all tasks finish, a timeout elapses, or the thread is interrupted. Essential for clean shutdown.

questions.questionHtml: What is the key difference between Callable and Runnable?
options: Callable can be submitted to an ExecutorService; Runnable cannot
Callable's call() method returns a value and can throw checked exceptions
Runnable is faster because it uses less memory
Callable requires a thread pool; Runnable can run on any thread
questions.correctAnswer: Callable's call() method returns a value and can throw checked exceptions
questions.explanationHtml: Callable<V>.call() returns V and can throw any exception. Runnable.run() returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions. Both can be submitted to an ExecutorService.
A single-thread executor runs tasks sequentially in submission order. f1 completes before f2. Both get() calls block briefly then return the results in order: Alpha, then Beta.

questions.questionHtml: What is wrong with this shutdown code?
questions.correctAnswer: shutdownNow() cancels running tasks; use shutdown() then awaitTermination() to let tasks complete gracefully
questions.explanationHtml: shutdownNow() attempts to interrupt running tasks immediately — some tasks may never complete. The correct approach: pool.shutdown() (stop accepting new tasks) followed by pool.awaitTermination(timeout, unit) (wait for remaining tasks to finish).

questions.questionHtml: You have a task that calls an external web service (blocking I/O) and you expect 100 concurrent calls. Which pool configuration is most appropriate?
options: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors())
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50) or higher, tuned to expected concurrency
Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()
new Thread() per request
questions.correctAnswer: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50) or higher, tuned to expected concurrency
questions.explanationHtml: CPU-bound tasks: pool size ≈ CPU cores (threads would just context-switch otherwise). I/O-bound tasks: threads spend most time waiting, so a larger pool is warranted — often 2–10× core count, tuned by measurement. A single-thread executor would serialize all 100 calls.

subChunks.title: CompletableFuture Basics
subChunks.hookHtml: Raw Future.get() blocks your thread like a stone wall. CompletableFuture lets you chain transformations, attach callbacks, and compose async pipelines — all without blocking a single thread.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Creating a CompletableFuture

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() runs a Supplier on the common ForkJoin pool (or a provided executor) and returns a CompletableFuture<T> you can chain. CompletableFuture.runAsync() does the same for Runnable (returns CompletableFuture<Void>).

CompletableFuture<String> cf = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    // runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
    return "Arcane";
});

Transforming Results: thenApply, thenAccept, thenRun

These methods attach callbacks that execute when the future completes. They form a pipeline — each receives the previous stage's result.

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Arcane")
    .thenApply(s -> s + " Surge")          // transforms: String -> String
    .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)          // transforms: "ARCANE SURGE"
    .thenAccept(s -> System.out.println("Result: " + s)) // consumes, returns Void
    .thenRun(() -> System.out.println("Pipeline complete")); // no input, no output

join() vs get()

Both block the calling thread until the result is available. The difference: get() throws checked exceptions (InterruptedException, ExecutionException), forcing you to handle them. join() wraps exceptions in unchecked CompletionException — cleaner in lambda chains.

String result = cf.join(); // unchecked — cleaner in pipelines
// vs
String result2 = cf.get(); // throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException

Error Handling: exceptionally & whenComplete

exceptionally() catches any exception in the pipeline and returns a fallback value — like a catch block for async code. whenComplete() runs a callback with either the result OR the exception (similar to finally).

CompletableFuture<String> safe = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("Spell fizzled!"); })
    .exceptionally(ex -> "Default Spell"); // fallback value on error

safe.thenAccept(System.out::println); // prints "Default Spell"
safe.join();

completeExceptionally & Manual Completion

You can manually complete a CompletableFuture with complete(value) or fail it with completeExceptionally(throwable). This is useful when bridging callback-based APIs into the CompletableFuture world.

CompletableFuture<String> manual = new CompletableFuture<>();
// somewhere later, after async work finishes:
manual.complete("Result ready");
// or on failure:
manual.completeExceptionally(new RuntimeException("Failed"));

storyBeats.text: The Academy's ancient scrying orbs could only show one vision at a time — each mage had to wait, blocking the chamber, until the orb went dark before the next could look. A new invention changed everything.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: CompletableFuture is the modern crystal ball. Instead of staring into it until an answer appears — blocking all else — you attach instructions for what to do when the vision arrives, then walk away.

storyBeats.speaker: Async Pipeline
storyBeats.text:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Arcane")
    .thenApply(s -> s + " Surge")
    .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)
    .thenAccept(System.out::println)
    .join();

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: thenApply transforms the result — like an alchemist changing lead to gold. thenAccept consumes it — like delivering the gold to the vault. thenRun fires afterward with no regard for the result.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And when a spell goes wrong, exceptionally() catches the disaster and returns a safe fallback. Never let an unhandled exception shatter your pipeline.

storyBeats.speaker: Error Handling
storyBeats.text:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw new RuntimeException(); })
    .exceptionally(ex -> "Default Spell")
    .thenAccept(System.out::println)
    .join(); // prints "Default Spell"
With CompletableFuture, the scrying chamber handles dozens of visions simultaneously — no mage standing idle, each vision feeding the next step of the arcane pipeline automatically.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a CompletableFuture pipeline: use supplyAsync to supply the string "Arcane". Chain thenApply to append " Surge". Chain another thenApply to convert to uppercase. Chain thenAccept to print "Final spell: " + the result. Chain thenRun to print "Pipeline complete". Call .join() at the end of the chain to block until done.

Also demonstrate exceptionally: create a separate future that throws a RuntimeException, use .exceptionally(e -> "Spell fizzled"), join it, and print the result.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between thenApply, thenAccept, and thenRun. When would you use exceptionally() versus whenComplete()? And explain why join() is often preferred over get() inside lambda chains.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, build a CompletableFuture pipeline: supplyAsync("Arcane"), append " Surge", uppercase, print "Final spell: ARCANE SURGE", then print "Pipeline complete". Also create a second future that throws an exception, handle it with exceptionally to return "Spell fizzled", and print that result.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The default thread pool used by supplyAsync() and runAsync() when no executor is provided. Shared JVM-wide; fine for CPU tasks but avoid for blocking I/O (use a dedicated pool instead).
The interface CompletableFuture implements, defining the chainable methods (thenApply, thenAccept, etc.). Allows swapping implementations without changing pipeline code.
Like thenApply() but executes the transformation on a separate thread from the pool, rather than on the thread that completed the previous stage.
A two-argument callback receiving both the result and the exception (one will be null). Unlike exceptionally(), handle() runs regardless of success or failure and can transform both cases.
The unchecked exception join() throws (wrapping the original cause) when the CompletableFuture completed exceptionally. Access the real cause via getCause().
The challenge of slowing a producer when consumers can't keep up. CompletableFuture has no built-in backpressure — for that, explore reactive libraries like Project Reactor or RxJava.
A modern approach (previewed in Java 21+) where async tasks have a clear scope and lifetime tied to a parent task. Aims to make concurrent code safer and easier to reason about than raw futures.
Java 21 feature (Project Loom) — lightweight threads managed by the JVM. Blocking virtual threads is cheap, reducing the need for async pipelines for I/O-bound work.

questions.questionHtml: Which CompletableFuture method consumes the result (returns CompletableFuture<Void>) without transforming it?
options: thenApply()
thenAccept()
thenRun()
thenCompose()
questions.explanationHtml: thenAccept(Consumer) receives the result and performs a side effect, returning CompletableFuture<Void>. thenApply(Function) transforms the result. thenRun(Runnable) ignores the result entirely.
Start with 10, multiply by 3 → 30, add 5 → 35. The thenAccept prints "Value: 35".

questions.questionHtml: This code should print a fallback when an exception occurs, but it throws instead. What is wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: exceptionally() is missing — add .exceptionally(ex -> "Fallback") before join()
questions.explanationHtml: join() rethrows the exception as a CompletionException if the future completed exceptionally. Add .exceptionally(ex -> "Fallback") before join() to catch the error and return a default value.

questions.questionHtml: When should you provide a custom Executor to supplyAsync(supplier, executor) instead of using the default common pool?
options: When the task is CPU-bound and fast
When the task performs blocking I/O such as database or network calls
When you want the task to run on the main thread
When using thenApply() chains
questions.correctAnswer: When the task performs blocking I/O such as database or network calls
questions.explanationHtml: The common ForkJoinPool is sized for CPU-bound work. Blocking I/O tasks submitted there can starve other async tasks. Use a dedicated ExecutorService for I/O-bound work so blocking threads don't clog the shared pool.

subChunks.title: Combining & Composing Futures
subChunks.hookHtml: One arcane calculation at a time is never enough. Real spells combine multiple async results — weaving damage rolls, defence checks, and element lookups into a single decisive outcome.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
thenCompose — Chaining Dependent Futures

thenCompose() is the flatMap of CompletableFuture. Use it when the next step itself returns a CompletableFuture — otherwise you'd get CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>> with thenApply.

CompletableFuture<String> spellName = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Fire");
CompletableFuture<String> fullSpell = spellName.thenCompose(name ->
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> name + "ball") // another async step
);
System.out.println(fullSpell.join()); // "Fireball"

thenCombine — Zipping Two Independent Futures

thenCombine(other, BiFunction) waits for both futures to complete independently, then combines their results. The two futures run in parallel.

CompletableFuture<Integer> damage  = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 70);
CompletableFuture<Integer> defense = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 30);

CompletableFuture<Integer> netDamage = damage.thenCombine(defense,
    (dmg, def) -> dmg - def
);
System.out.println("Net damage: " + netDamage.join()); // "Net damage: 40"

allOf — Wait for Everything

CompletableFuture.allOf(cf1, cf2, ...) returns a CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when ALL supplied futures complete. Useful for fan-out then collect patterns.

CompletableFuture<String> f1 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "A");
CompletableFuture<String> f2 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "B");
CompletableFuture<String> f3 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "C");

CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3).join(); // wait for all
System.out.println(f1.join() + f2.join() + f3.join()); // "ABC" (order guaranteed now)

anyOf — First to Complete Wins

CompletableFuture.anyOf(cf1, cf2, ...) returns a CompletableFuture<Object> that completes as soon as the first of the supplied futures completes. Useful for racing redundant requests.

CompletableFuture<Object> fastest = CompletableFuture.anyOf(
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Slow spell"),
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Fast spell")
);
System.out.println(fastest.join()); // whichever finishes first

whenComplete — Cleanup Callback

whenComplete(BiConsumer<T, Throwable>) runs a callback with either the result or exception (one is null), without transforming the value. It's always executed, like a finally block, making it ideal for logging or releasing resources.

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Spell cast")
    .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
        if (ex != null) System.out.println("Failed: " + ex.getMessage());
        else System.out.println("Success: " + result);
    })
    .join();

storyBeats.text: The Grand Duel required three simultaneous calculations — damage roll, defense roll, and elemental affinity — each drawn from a different arcane register. No single oracle could provide all three.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: thenCombine is your spell for zipping two independent futures. Both oracles consult simultaneously, and when both reply, you merge their answers into a single truth.

storyBeats.speaker: thenCombine
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: allOf waits for every oracle to report. anyOf names the winner of a race. Choose wisely — waiting for all is thorough; racing to the first is fast but unpredictable.

storyBeats.speaker: allOf Pattern
storyBeats.text:
CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3).join();
System.out.println("All spells resolved");

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: thenCompose is flatMap — use it when your next step itself returns a future. Without it, you'd have a future inside a future, like a scroll sealed inside another scroll.
The Grand Duel resolved cleanly: damage and defense calculated in parallel, combined in milliseconds, the net damage printed to the scoreboard before the dust settled.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Part 1: Create futureA = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 70) (damage) and futureB = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 30) (defense). Use thenCombine to compute damage - defense and print "Net damage: " + the result. Call join().

Part 2: Create 3 separate futures using supplyAsync. Use CompletableFuture.allOf() to wait for all three. After allOf().join(), print "All spells resolved".
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between thenApply and thenCompose with a concrete example. When would combining two futures with thenCombine be better than running them sequentially? What does allOf return and why can't you get the individual results from it directly?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, create two CompletableFutures: one supplying 70 (damage) and one supplying 30 (defense). Combine them with thenCombine to compute damage minus defense, then print "Net damage: " + result. Also create 3 futures and use allOf to wait for all, then print "All spells resolved".

rabbitHoleTerms.description: thenApply wraps the returned value in a new future (use for synchronous transforms). thenCompose flattens a returned future — use when your callback itself returns a CompletableFuture, avoiding nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>.
allOf() returns CompletableFuture<Void> — you can't get results from it directly. Pattern: after allOf.join(), call join() on each individual future (they're all done at that point).
anyOf() returns the result of the first completing future but does not cancel the others — they continue running. Use carefully if tasks have side effects.
Like thenCombine but runs the BiFunction on a thread from the pool instead of the completing thread. Prefer when the combining logic is heavy.
Java 21 introduced virtual threads that make blocking I/O cheap. Much async code written with CompletableFuture could be simplified to straightforward blocking code on virtual threads.
A specification (implemented by Project Reactor, RxJava) for async stream processing with backpressure. CompletableFuture handles single-value async; reactive handles streams of values.
Non-async thenApply/thenAccept run on the thread that completed the previous stage. Async variants (thenApplyAsync) run on the pool. Mixing these can cause subtle ordering issues.
Java 9+ method on CompletableFuture that completes the future exceptionally with TimeoutException after a given duration — cleaner than manually scheduling cancellation.

options: CompletableFuture<List<Object>> containing all results
CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all futures complete
CompletableFuture<Object> containing the first result

questions.correctAnswer: CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all futures complete

questions.questionHtml: This code tries to chain two async operations but ends up with a nested future. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
questions.correctAnswer: Replace thenApply with thenCompose to flatten the nested future
questions.explanationHtml: When the mapper in thenApply itself returns a CompletableFuture, you get CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>. Use thenCompose instead — it flattens the result to CompletableFuture<T>.

questions.questionHtml: You need to call two independent services and combine their results. Which approach is most efficient?
options: Call service A with supplyAsync, join(), then call service B with supplyAsync, join(), then combine
Use thenCombine with two supplyAsync calls so both run in parallel
Use thenCompose to chain service A then service B sequentially
Create a single supplyAsync that calls both services sequentially
questions.correctAnswer: Use thenCombine with two supplyAsync calls so both run in parallel
questions.explanationHtml: thenCombine with two independent supplyAsync calls runs both in parallel, halving the total wait time compared to sequential calls. Calling join() between calls forces sequential execution, losing the parallelism benefit.
